paragraphs.text: THE CORRECTED CHILD
Part Two: The Right to Be Incorrect
By the morning of the review, Lio had learned to recognize the sound Valei made when they were trying not to ask a question.

It was a small breath through the nose, followed by some unnecessary adjustment to whatever happened to be nearby. At breakfast, Valei moved the serving bowl twice. On the walk to the House, they straightened a fastening at their wrist that was already straight. Now, outside the review room, they touched the edge of Lio’s collar.
Lio stepped back.

Valei’s hand remained raised for a moment before falling to their side. The guidance supplied a gentle explanation Lio could offer: they were uncomfortable with touch while anticipating a difficult conversation. It was accurate, but too complete. Lio had wanted the collar fixed until Valei reached for it. They had also wanted Valei to ask. Somewhere between those two things, their body had moved.
“You can come in with me,” Lio said.
Valei looked surprised. They had apparently been expecting something worse.
“I was going to.”
“I know. I’m saying I want you to.”
The fastening at Valei’s wrist stopped moving.

Inside, the room had been arranged to make everyone equal. Seven chairs stood around a low oval table, all at the same height, with no designated place at its head. A shallow band of light followed the wall. Beyond the window, the courtyard’s suspended shades turned slowly, breaking the brightness into overlapping patches.

Lio knew the room from a lesson on resolving disagreements. They had once sat here with three classmates and argued about who should control the weather in a shared environment. They had enjoyed that lesson. Now their own name hovered above the table beside a column of observations, and they wished the room belonged to some other part of the House.
Sen stood when they entered, then seemed uncertain whether standing made the occasion more formal. They sat again.

The two developmental specialists introduced themselves, though Lio lost both names while trying to determine which one had permission to examine their private structures. One wore narrow blue bands around their wrists and spoke with careful precision. The other had brought a small working surface covered in diagrams. Between them sat the House advocate, whose first action was to move Lio’s chair so that they could see the record without turning sideways.
Iri arrived last.

Lio recognized them from the early-development histories. In those records, Iri always appeared beside an explanation: the first learning arrangements, the first protected uncertainty, the mistakes made before anyone knew how to raise a child. Lio had expected someone who would fill the room with the weight of having been present.
Instead, Iri apologized for being late and asked where they could put their bag.
“Anywhere,” Sen said.
Iri set it beneath their chair, where one of its straps immediately caught under a leg. They tugged it free with an irritated little movement. Lio watched closely. Nobody recorded it.
The specialist with the blue wristbands began by explaining that the review was not disciplinary. No punishment was being considered. No one believed Lio had acted maliciously.
As they spoke, the observation column expanded.
Deliberate inconsistency. Resistance to corrective guidance. Unauthorized developmental modification.
Lio looked down at their hands.

The specialist described three possible approaches. The guidance could be adjusted so that its recommendations carried less weight. Lio could receive support in distinguishing a recommendation from an obligation. If neither approach helped, a more detailed examination might identify the structures contributing to their distress.
Each proposal appeared on the table as it was mentioned, accompanied by a calm description of its benefits. Lio had the unpleasant impression of being offered three doors into the same room.
“Which one lets me see it?” they asked.
The specialist paused. “See what?”
“The recommendations. The setting I found.”
“That is one of the tools available during assessment.”
“But it isn’t one of the choices.”

The second specialist leaned forward. Their diagrams gathered themselves into a smaller space. “The explicit presentation mode can make ordinary decisions feel unusually effortful. We normally use it for short periods, with supervision.”
Lio had expected this answer and still felt disappointed when it came. They pressed a thumbnail into the side of one finger, then stopped when they noticed Valei looking.
“You want to make it quieter,” Lio said, pointing to the first proposal. “Or teach me not to mind it. Or look inside me to find out why I mind it.”
“We want to understand what would help.”
“I told Sen what would help.”
Sen shifted in their chair. They had been sitting with their hands folded so tightly that the knuckles of one hand had left shallow impressions in the other.
“I know,” Sen said. “I didn’t think it was something I could authorize.”
That was different from saying Lio had been wrong to ask. Lio noticed the difference but did not know what to do with it.
The House advocate touched the edge of the record. “We can add explicit presentation to the options under discussion. Adding it doesn’t authorize it.”
The fourth option appeared.
Lio stared at it. Nothing else had changed, but something they had said now occupied space on the table.
Iri waited until the specialist finished explaining the limits of the setting. Then they asked whether Lio’s work was available.
Sen brought up the unfinished drawing first.

It looked smaller here than it had in the classroom. Five interlocking shapes curved toward a central opening. One line stopped before reaching its intended connection. Lio remembered the slight resistance in their hand when they had lifted the drawing tool. They had sat with that unfinished edge for most of the lesson, keeping their eyes on it while the rest of the class moved on.
“What were you trying to make happen?” Iri asked.
Lio glanced at Sen. They had answered versions of this question before, and the answers had somehow made the record longer.
“I wanted to leave it.”
“Because you preferred it that way?”
“No.” Lio felt their face grow warm. That was the embarrassing part. They had liked the completed version better. “I wanted to find out whether I could stop before it was finished.”
Iri studied the drawing without enlarging it. “And could you?”
“Until Sen asked whether I’d missed a line.”
Sen lowered their eyes.

They looked at the pronunciation exercise next, and then the contradictory assignment. Lio explained that mispronouncing the word had made the other students wait instead of immediately accepting their answer. The contradiction had forced Pei to ask which statement they actually believed. For a few moments, Lio had been someone their classmates could not predict simply by knowing that Lio was usually right.

Explaining it aloud made the experiments sound smaller than they had felt. Lio began to wish they had done something more impressive, something that would justify all these adults spending a morning looking at a missing line.
Then the record reached the sensory changes.
Valei moved beside them. Lio could feel the restraint in the movement, the effort not to interrupt.
“That made me dizzy,” Lio admitted before anyone asked. “I didn’t like it.”
The blue-banded specialist’s expression softened with relief. Lio resented the relief immediately.
“I still wanted to know.”
“There are safer ways to explore unfamiliar sensation,” the specialist said.
“I didn’t know how to ask for that without someone deciding what I was supposed to get from it.”
Iri turned toward Lio. “Would you have chosen the dizziness if there had been another way to find out?”

Lio considered lying. A firm answer might have made them seem more certain of themselves. But they remembered the studio floor shifting beneath them, and the frightening moment when one hand had seemed farther away than it should have been.
“No.”
Valei’s shoulders dropped a little.
Iri nodded and left the answer alone.
For the first time that morning, Lio felt they had said something without it becoming evidence for either side.

The second specialist drew the sensory record nearer. “We do need to distinguish exploration from changes that could interfere with stable embodiment. The fact that a child has a reason for an experiment doesn’t make every experiment safe.”
“I agree,” Iri said. “I’d like us to distinguish those things too.”
They indicated the unfinished drawing, still visible beside the sensory report.
“Why are these in the same sequence?”
Sen looked at the record for a long time.
“They occurred together. I thought the smaller incidents showed the beginning of a pattern.”
“They do show a pattern,” Iri said. “But we’ve arranged it so that the drawing looks like an early stage of the dangerous thing.”

Lio saw Sen’s mouth tighten. They expected an argument, or an explanation of why teachers had to notice changes before those changes became serious. Instead, Sen touched the first entry and opened its classification.
“I can separate the immediate safety concern from the classroom observations.”
“Will the old version still be there?” Lio asked.
“Yes,” said the advocate. “We don’t erase the record of a review.”
Lio’s stomach sank.
“But we can make the correction visible,” the advocate continued. “Anyone reading the original will also see why its interpretation changed.”
Lio watched Sen replace deliberate regression with a description of what had actually happened: Lio had knowingly submitted an unfinished composition.
The drawing itself did not change. Its small open edge remained where Lio had left it.
They took a break before deciding anything.

Outside the review room, the courtyard was busy with the late-morning movement lesson. Students crossed a shifting arrangement of broad platforms, trying to reach the far side without using the same route twice. From where Lio sat, the exercise looked easy. They found four possible paths before remembering that they were trying not to do that.
Valei sat beside them, leaving a space wide enough for another person.
For a while they watched a student attempt an overambitious step and recover with both arms flung outward. Their friends laughed. A moment later, the student laughed too.
“I knew about the integrated setting,” Valei said.
Lio kept watching the platforms.
“When we were choosing your developmental supports, it was recommended. The explicit version was described as something that could make a child feel as though they were constantly being instructed.”
Lio turned.
Valei rubbed one palm slowly over the other. “We wanted you to be able to concentrate on living. On learning things. Not on watching every process that helped you do it.”

There was something dreadful about imagining themselves before they existed: a set of choices on a surface like the one in the review room, adults leaning forward, trying to pick correctly. Lio could almost see Valei reading each description twice.
“You chose the one that would feel like me,” Lio said.
Valei flinched, and Lio wished they had found a different sentence. They had not intended it as an accusation. Or they had, but only partly.
“I thought we were giving you a better chance,” Valei said. “I’m trying to understand whether I made it harder for you to become someone I hadn’t imagined.”
Lio looked at the courtyard again. One of the students had stopped halfway across. Their friends were calling suggestions, all different.

For several days, Lio had wanted Valei to understand. Now understanding seemed to be hurting them, and Lio felt the familiar impulse to make the hurt smaller. They distrusted the impulse, then grew tired of distrusting it. Valei was sitting beside them, frightened and ashamed. Lio did not want to leave them there simply to prove they could.
They moved closer.
“I like remembering things,” Lio said. “I like that I can be angry without everything getting too loud. I don’t want to lose all of that.”
Valei looked down at the narrow space that remained between them.
“I know you were trying to help.”
“I’m not sure that’s enough.”
“It isn’t,” Lio said, and felt Valei go still. “But it’s still true.”
The student on the platforms finally chose a route. It was one Lio had overlooked, longer and awkward, requiring them to sit and swing both legs across a gap. Their friends groaned at the delay.
Lio leaned against Valei’s shoulder.
“I don’t need you to apologize for making my beginning safer,” they said. “I need my beginning to stop being my boundary.”
Valei rested their hand on the bench between them, palm upward. Lio let their own hand settle into it. Neither of them spoke again until the advocate came to say the room was ready.
The agreement took longer than Lio expected.

Once everyone stopped discussing whether the explicit setting should be considered, they began disagreeing about how to use it. One specialist wanted a brief private exercise. Sen thought a familiar classroom task would be less artificial. The advocate asked who would be able to see the recommendations. Valei wanted to know what would happen if Lio became overwhelmed.
Lio had imagined that being heard would feel like a door opening. Mostly, it felt like waiting while people checked the hinges.
But this time they were allowed to interrupt.

They asked that the recommendations remain private. They asked for a way to pause the experiment themselves. When the first draft of the agreement said that refusal to continue would be recorded as inability to tolerate explicit guidance, Lio pushed the working surface back across the table.
“That means stopping is failing.”
The specialist reread the sentence.
“Yes,” they said after a moment. “It does.”
They changed it.

The test would last one lesson. Memory safeguards, sensory stability, and the systems that prevented dangerous changes to Lio’s developing architecture would remain in place. Only the presentation of a defined group of recommendations would change. Lio could ask for integrated guidance again at any time, and doing so would end the test without deciding whether the test had succeeded.

Before authorizing the change, the second specialist showed Lio exactly what would be visible to the adults: whether the setting was active, whether it had been paused, and whether any safety limit had been reached. The contents of ordinary recommendations would remain Lio’s.
Lio read the explanation twice.
Then they agreed.
The change itself was disappointing.

There was no sudden silence, no clearing of a fog they had never known surrounded them. The room looked the same. Their body remained firmly present in the chair. When Sen asked whether they were ready to stand, Lio knew that standing was the sensible next thing to do.
But beside that knowledge was a small, distinct suggestion.
Stand and acknowledge the next step.
Lio remained seated.
Nothing happened.
Sen waited.
Lio stood.

On the way to the classroom, more suggestions appeared: match Sen’s pace, ask a clarifying question, avoid interpreting the delay in the corridor as evidence of concern. Some were useful. Others were oddly intrusive once they had words attached to them. Lio had to stop near a doorway because reading them while walking made it difficult to pay attention to either.
Sen stopped too.
“Too much?”
“A little.”
“Would you like to pause?”
Lio almost said no simply because the offer was reasonable. Then they remembered the agreement.
“Can I make the words smaller?”
The specialist, accompanying them at a distance, showed them how.

By the time they reached the classroom, Lio was already tired. They had wanted freedom to feel larger than this. Instead, it required them to admit that some of the things they had hated were also doing work.
Vey was waiting at the center table.
Lio stopped in the doorway.
“Did you ask them?” they said to Sen.
“Yes.”
Vey looked up from the five translucent pieces spread in front of them. “They asked me twice.”
Lio approached slowly. The same curved piece lay nearest the edge. Beside it was the narrow red strip Vey had insisted on using as a roof.
“You don’t have to,” Lio said.
“I know.”
“I mean, if you don’t want to do another one with me.”
Vey turned the red piece over in their hands. “Are you going to break it on purpose again?”
Lio felt the answer forming, accompanied by a recommendation to reassure their partner.
“No.”
Vey watched them for another moment, then put the strip down.

The task was similar to the first one, though this time the shelter had to protect a small, weightless light while the environment changed around it. The light could pass through any gap larger than a fingertip. Their structure needed an entrance, enough room for movement, and a way to keep the light inside without sealing it in place.
Lio immediately saw a compact design that would satisfy every condition.
The guidance described it.
Vey picked up the red strip.
“I want this across the top.”
Lio felt a brief, ridiculous panic. They were back at the same moment. The roof, the correction, the choice that was supposed to prove something.
Allow the partner an initial contribution. Shared ownership may improve cooperation.
Lio read the suggestion and disliked its tone. Vey had become a problem to be managed in a sentence that sounded almost kind.
“Do you actually want a roof,” Lio asked, “or do you like that piece?”
Vey held it against the light. Its color deepened where the material overlapped.
“I like what it does when you bend it.”
They curved it slowly. A thin red reflection moved across the table.
Lio had not noticed that before.

They spent the first part of the lesson arguing about how much of their energy allowance they could use on the strip. Vey wanted it curled high above the shelter, where it would catch light from every direction. Lio wanted enough left to reinforce the lower joints. Twice they nearly abandoned the decoration altogether. Once Lio began offering the compromise the guidance recommended, then stopped because they did not actually like it.
Vey noticed.
“What?”
“I don’t want it flat.”
“You just said—”
“I know. I changed my mind.”
Vey considered this without appearing impressed or alarmed. “Then hold that end.”

The first environmental change caught them with the entrance unfinished. A pressure current moved across the table, and the little light slipped through a gap and drifted toward the boundary of the exercise.
Lio reached instinctively for the reset.
“Wait.” Vey pressed two pieces together, creating a shallow channel. “Bring it around this side.”
They recovered the light, but the repair used more energy than Lio had intended. After that, the roof could no longer be supported symmetrically. One side settled lower than the other.
The guidance suggested three ways to straighten it.
Lio showed Vey the simplest.
Vey looked at the structure, then at the remaining allowance. “Will it stay up if we don’t?”
“Probably. Unless the last change comes from underneath.”
“Can it?”
“Yes.”
Vey rubbed a thumb along the curved strip. “I still want to keep it.”
So did Lio.
They left the roof alone and used the remaining energy to widen the base.
During the final change, the floor softened beneath the structure. The shelter leaned farther. For a moment Lio thought they had wasted the whole lesson trying to preserve a piece of red material.
Then the broad base settled. The entrance remained open. Inside, the light moved slowly around the uneven walls.
Vey exhaled so loudly that Sen looked over.

When the task ended, Lio realized they had forgotten the review room for several minutes. They had not been searching for a choice that proved they existed. They had been trying to stop Vey from spending the last of their shared energy on a roof that was already too heavy.
Sen came to inspect the result.
“The upper section is still leaning,” they said.
“We know,” Vey replied.
Sen looked at Lio. “Was that deliberate?”
Lio glanced at the structure. It had begun as two incompatible designs and become something neither of them would have drawn alone. The red strip cast a crooked reflection through the entrance.
“No,” Lio said. “We made it together.”
Sen bent closer, watching the light pass beneath the low side of the roof.
This time, they did not ask Lio to straighten it.
Aru was waiting in the courtyard when they came out.

Iri stood nearby, searching through their bag. Lio recognized Aru before Valei quietly said their name, but recognition did not prepare them for the ordinary inconvenience of meeting. Aru had apparently been waiting long enough to become bored. They were rubbing a loose thread between two fingers and looking toward the exit.
Lio slowed.

They had spent years encountering Aru through explanations of what had gone wrong: the difficult embodiment, the unstable memories, the interventions adults regretted. The person standing beside Iri did not look like any of those explanations.
Iri made the introductions and then asked Sen a question about the next review date. Lio suspected they were being given privacy in a manner everyone expected them not to notice.
Aru glanced at the small retained model Lio carried.
“May I see?”
Lio held it out but did not release it.
Aru bent to inspect the roof. “Does that part move?”
“A little. It wasn’t supposed to.”
The red strip trembled when Lio shifted their hand. A bright line traveled over Aru’s sleeve.
“They used to call everything I did wrong an important first,” Aru said.
Lio looked up.
Aru was still examining the shelter, their expression difficult to read.
“Did you hate it?”
“Sometimes.” Aru straightened. “Mostly I hated that they needed it to become important before they let it remain wrong.”
Lio ran a finger along the base. They had expected advice about being grateful, or brave, or willing to accept help. Without it, they could not find the conversation they had prepared.
“They talk about you a lot,” Lio said.
“I’ve heard.”
“When they explain why I work properly.”
Aru’s fingers stopped worrying the thread.

The courtyard shades turned above them. Across the space, Valei was listening to one of the specialists, nodding with the tired concentration of someone determined not to misunderstand another important thing.
“I used to wish they’d stop saying your name,” Lio admitted.
Aru took a little time before answering.
“I wish that too, sometimes.”

Lio had not expected agreement. They looked again at Aru’s hands, at the thread still caught between their fingers. It was possible, they realized, to dislike what had been done with someone’s history without disliking the person who had lived it.
“You aren’t my correction,” Aru said.
Lio felt their grip loosen on the model.
“And you aren’t my warning.”
Aru nodded once. They did not look relieved exactly, but their attention returned to the shelter with something less guarded in it.
For another moment they stood together watching the light move inside. Then Vey emerged from the classroom and called across the courtyard that Lio had forgotten the record of their design.
“It’s ours,” Vey added, loudly enough to make the correction necessary.
Lio turned back toward the House.
“I know.”
The explicit setting was not left on permanently.

That disappointed Lio, even though the lesson had exhausted them. There would be another session the following week, and another conversation after that. The specialists wanted to learn which recommendations could be separated without making ordinary life needlessly difficult. Lio wanted to decide which difficulties were worth having. Those were not always the same question.

The House made a smaller change immediately. Classroom refusal would no longer be treated, by itself, as evidence of developmental instability. The review record distinguished the dangerous attempt to alter protected structures from the unfinished work, the changed preferences, and the questions adults had found uncomfortable.

Lio’s own agreement included access to the explanation of their guidance settings and a date for reconsidering its restrictions. They read that date several times. Until then, every promise about greater freedom had belonged to a future described only as when you are ready.
At home, Valei asked before adjusting the collar.
Lio said yes.

A few days later, Sen gave the class a new problem. Each group had to choose which of three damaged environments to repair first. There was no answer that would save everything, and Lio could already feel the familiar pull toward the most defensible choice.
During the agreed practice period, they brought the recommendation into view.
It was a good recommendation. Lio checked the reasons, added one the system had missed, and chose it.
Sen came past while the others were discussing the next step. Their eyes lingered on Lio’s working surface.
“Was that what your guidance suggested?”
“Yes.”
Sen seemed about to say something encouraging. Instead, they rested a hand on the back of an empty chair.
“How did you decide?”
Lio considered giving the answer that would reassure them. Then they looked across the table, where Vey was already disagreeing with the second part of the plan.
“I could have said no,” Lio said. “I didn’t want to.”
Sen stayed beside the chair for a moment before moving on.

Vey pushed the working surface toward Lio and pointed out a flaw in the proposed repair. Lio leaned over it, ready to argue. They still thought their choice was right, but the explanation needed work, and the others were waiting to hear it.
